lesson.title: The Constant Drip: How Leaky Bucket Enforces a Rigid Output Rate
lesson.summary: Leaky bucket shaping queues incoming packets and releases them at an absolutely constant rate, fully smoothing away burstiness instead of banking and permitting it the way token bucket does.
lesson.body:
The leaky bucket algorithm takes its name from an intuitive picture: water, representing arriving packets, is poured into a bucket at whatever rate the source happens to produce it, which may be very bursty. The bucket has a hole in the bottom and leaks at a fixed rate, regardless of how much water is currently sitting inside, as long as there is at least some water there to leak. If water is poured in faster than the bucket's total capacity can absorb, the overflow is simply lost, which corresponds to dropped packets when the shaping queue is full.

The contrast with token bucket, covered in the previous chapter, is precise and worth tracing through the exact same numbers. Token bucket's output could burst up to the bucket size b instantaneously, because unused tokens could be saved up while the sender was idle. Leaky bucket's output is capped at a fixed rate at every single instant, no matter how much backlog is queued and no matter how idle the link was beforehand. Take the same burst of six packets arriving at t equals 0, now shaped by a leaky bucket with a leak rate of 2 packets per second. Packet 1 does not depart at t equals 0, it must wait for the first drip, departing at t equals 0.5. Packet 2 departs at t equals 1.0, packet 3 at t equals 1.5, packet 4 at t equals 2.0, packet 5 at t equals 2.5, and packet 6 at t equals 3.0. Compare that departure sequence, 0.5, 1.0, 1.5, 2.0, 2.5, 3.0, against token bucket's sequence for the identical input burst, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0.5, 1.0. Both converge to the same long-run rate of 2 packets per second, but the short-term behavior is completely different: token bucket let the first four packets out immediately with no delay at all, while leaky bucket held every single packet, including the very first one, to a strict half-second spacing.

That rigidity is exactly what makes leaky bucket the right tool in situations where a downstream link or device genuinely cannot tolerate bursts. A legacy constant-bit-rate circuit, or a downstream device with a very small buffer, or jitter-intolerant hardware sitting right after the shaper, may need perfectly even spacing far more than it needs low average delay. Leaky bucket accepts a worse best case, since even the very first packet in an idle burst is delayed, in exchange for a guarantee that output is never, ever burstier than the configured rate.

Put the two side by side and the trade-off is easy to state. Token bucket is bursty but bounded: it gives better average latency, especially to senders who were recently idle, and it does not penalize a flow simply for having been quiet, which is why it is the more common default for general-purpose traffic shaping. Leaky bucket is strictly regular: every packet pays the same delay tax in exchange for output that is smoother than token bucket can ever guarantee, which is worth it whenever a perfectly constant rate matters more than minimizing any individual packet's delay.
